title: Confidence Interval for the Difference of Population Proportions
videoTitle: AP Statistics Topics 3.10 and 3.11 Confidence Interval for the Difference of Population Proportions
intro: After this lesson you can name and set up a two-sample $z$ interval for $p_1-p_2$, verify its conditions, compute the interval, interpret it and the confidence level in context, and decide whether it supports a claim about a difference.

moments.title: Estimating a difference of proportions
moments.text: A confidence interval based on two samples estimates $p_1-p_2$, using a two-sample $z$ interval.

moments.title: Registered voters in two states
moments.text: The parameter is a difference, estimated with one sample proportion from each state.

moments.title: Name and parameter in one sentence
moments.text: "A two-sample $z$ interval for $p_1-p_2$, the difference between the proportion of ... and the proportion of ..."

moments.title: Three conditions
moments.text: Randomization, 10% for each sample (random sampling only), and at least 10 successes and failures in each sample.

moments.title: No 10% check for experiments
moments.text: In a randomized experiment, the 10% condition does not apply.

moments.title: The interval
moments.text: $(\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm z^*\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$.

moments.title: Critical value from the confidence level
Interpreting the confidence level
moments.text: In repeated random sampling, about $C\%$ of intervals capture the true difference.

moments.title: Conclusion with endpoints in context
moments.text: "I am 95% confident that the difference between the proportion of ... and the proportion of ... is between ... and ..."

moments.title: Standard error, not standard deviation
moments.text: The formula uses sample proportions, so it estimates the standard deviation.

moments.title: Interpret a negative endpoint
moments.text: The interval (-0.1167, 0.0207) means Florida could be about 11.7 points lower or 2.1 points higher.

moments.title: Zero in the interval
moments.text: If 0 is in the interval, there is no convincing evidence of a difference.

moments.title: Does the interval justify the claim?
moments.text: An all-positive interval for new minus old supports a higher proportion for the new drug.

cards.name: All positive
cards.text: Convincing evidence that the first proportion is larger.

cards.name: All negative
cards.text: Convincing evidence that the first proportion is smaller.

cards.name: Contains 0
cards.text: No convincing evidence of a difference.

cells: Contains 0: no convincing evidence of a difference
All positive: new has the higher proportion
All negative: first proportion is smaller

notes.label: Wording check.
notes.text: Every value in the interval is a plausible value. Do not say "mostly negative so probably negative". Say whether 0 is plausible.

sections.title: PANIC for a two-sample z interval
sections.intro: Five steps. The name and the parameter fit in one sentence. Never skip the three conditions for both samples.
steps: Parameter and Name: "A two-sample $z$ interval for $p_1-p_2$, the difference between the proportion of ... in ... and ...".
Assumptions: random samples (or random assignment), each sample at most 10% of its population (not for experiments), at least 10 successes and 10 failures in each sample.
Conclusion: "I am $C\%$ confident that the difference between ... is between $a$ and $b$."

parts.label: Standard error
parts.text: Match each proportion with its own sample size.

sections.line: $(\hat p_1-\hat p_2)\pm z^*\sqrt{\dfrac{\hat p_1(1-\hat p_1)}{n_1}+\dfrac{\hat p_2(1-\hat p_2)}{n_2}}$

traps.title: Conclusion with the endpoints and the order
traps.weak: We are 95% confident the states are different.
traps.better: I am 95% confident that the difference between the proportion of Florida adults registered to vote and the proportion of Kentucky adults registered to vote is between -0.1167 and 0.0207.

traps.title: Interpreting the confidence level
traps.weak: There is a 95% chance the true difference is in this interval.
traps.better: In repeated random sampling with the same sample sizes from the same populations, about 95% of intervals created this way will capture the true difference in proportions.

traps.title: Using the 10% condition in an experiment
traps.weak: 400 is less than 10% of all migraine sufferers.
traps.better: The patients were randomly assigned, not randomly sampled, so the 10% condition does not apply. Check random assignment instead.

traps.title: Mismatching proportions and sample sizes
traps.better: Pair each proportion with its own sample size: $\sqrt{\frac{0.76(0.24)}{300}+\frac{0.808(0.192)}{250}}$.

traps.title: Zero in the interval
traps.weak: There is mostly negative values, so Florida is lower.
traps.better: The interval contains 0, so 0 is a plausible value for the difference. There is not convincing evidence that the proportions differ.

questions.stem: A 90% confidence interval for $p_A-p_B$ is (0.074, 0.233). Which conclusion is justified?
opts: There is no convincing evidence of a difference.
why: Correct. The whole interval is positive, so 0 is not plausible and $p_A$ is larger.
The interval is positive, so $A$ minus $B$ is positive.
The center 0.153 is only the estimate; the interval gives a range.

questions.stem: Which condition is NOT required for a two-sample $z$ interval from a randomized experiment?
opts: Each group is at most 10% of a population
At least 10 successes in each group
At least 10 failures in each group
why: Correct. There is no population sampled, so the 10% condition does not apply.

questions.stem: A 95% confidence interval for $p_1-p_2$ is (-0.137, 0.077). Which statement is correct?
opts: The interval contains 0, so 0 is a plausible difference
why: A confidence interval cannot prove equality.
A negative lower endpoint does not show the difference is negative.
Correct. Zero is inside the interval.

questions.stem: Which is the best interpretation of "95% confidence" for a two-sample interval?
opts: The true difference is in the interval 95% of the time
There is a 95% chance the sample is random
95% of the sample differences are inside the interval
About 95% of intervals from repeated random samples capture the true difference in proportions
why: The true difference is fixed. The interval is what varies.
Randomness is a condition, not something the confidence level measures.
The interval describes a population parameter, not the sample differences.
Correct. The confidence level describes the method over repeated random sampling.

sections.title: Free-response practice
sections.prompt: A principal wants to compare the proportion of students who walk to school at two campuses. A random sample of 200 students at campus A included 118 walkers, and an independent random sample of 220 students at campus B included 96 walkers. Assume each campus has more than 2,200 students.
parts: (a) State the name of the procedure and define the parameter.
(b) Verify the conditions for a 90% confidence interval.
(d) Interpret the interval in context and say whether it supports the claim that a higher proportion of campus A students walk.
sample: (a) A two-sample $z$ interval for $p_A-p_B$, where $p_A$ is the proportion of all students at campus A who walk and $p_B$ is the proportion of all students at campus B who walk.
(b) The samples are random and independent. 200 and 220 are under 10% of the campuses. Campus A: 118 walkers and 82 non-walkers. Campus B: 96 walkers and 124 non-walkers. All are at least 10.

(d) I am 90% confident that the proportion of campus A students who walk is between 7.4 and 23.3 percentage points higher than at campus B. The interval is entirely positive, so it supports the claim.
checklist: (a) Two-sample z interval and difference defined in context
(d) Uses the interval to decide the claim
